newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Busy tone as S.Africa phone company fights theft.
newsitem.headline: Busy tone as S.Africa phone company fights theft.

text.p: Thieves have stolen thousands of kilometres (miles) of copper cable from South Africa's state telecommunications utility in the past year, prompting calls for some radical solutions.
One anti-crime group suggests classifying copper as a precious metal, making it harder to deal in stolen cable.
Others say the phone company should stop providing a conventional phone system altogether and concentrate instead on creating an entirely cableless cellphone network.
Neither proposal has been leapt on by the state phone company, Telkom, which is South Africa's prime candidate for partial privatisation in the first part of this year.
But pressure for action is growing as business groups lose patience with sudden cuts in service inflicted by cable theft, which can leave a company phoneless for weeks in some cases.
Telkom says the scale of thievery has become a national problem, causing major service disruptions.
Even fibre-optic cable -- which has no blackmarket value -- is being ripped up by thieves looking for the $1.50 per kilo (2.2 pounds) that copper will bring, but who don't know the difference.
And it all has to be replaced.

Direct losses of copper cable totalled around 30 million rand ($6.6 million) in the last financial year. But this loss was dwarfed by the less obvious costs of replacement, lost revenue and loss of new business, Telkom says.

As one of its main long-term goals, Telkom is seeking an injection of private capital that would help it double the number of phone lines in South Africa, particularly into black communities long deprived of the convenience of the telephone.
Switching to an entirely cellular network, using mobile phones which are relatively expensive in South Africa, would hardly help meet this target.

Some African countries do limit infrastructure costs by using cellular telephone technology in their main cities. But putting phones in the hands of the better off only is not a politically acceptable course for South Africa's new democracy.
In the first three years of operation, mobile phone companies have hooked up some rural communities using microwave technology, but they principally serve the urban well-to-do.

The mobile phone is unlikely to get Telkom off the hook when it comes to serving bigger communities, such as the suburban shanty towns which cluster around South Africa's main cities. Many are still awaiting connection to power, water and sewerage services as well as normal telephones.

One business group concerned with crime has suggested that copper be declared a precious metal, so its trade would be limited to certified dealers, making it far more difficult to launder copper from illegal sources.

But metal dealer Len Davis, member of an industry group working on new legislation, says that would probably be going too far, because copper is not a precious metal. Davis, however, does favour some sort of regulation.

"We don't want to stop people from joining the trade, but we want them to be registered. Anyone who buys or generates copper scrap, from a second-hand car dealer...to a man with a wheelbarrow picking it up where he can, should be registered.
"We want a disciplined industry...where the trade is carried out in a responsible manner, he said.
Telkom has thrown its weight behind calls for a clamp-down on copper sales.
It has also set up a toll-free line for public tip-offs and now offers large rewards for information leading to arrest of the thieves.
Among those already caught are Telkom employees who have stolen the cable from company yards.
